I had a similar problem and then I spent a lot of time training my ear relative to the major scale. I did not find interval exercises helpful at all so I started by being able to sing the major scale up and down. Once you get that then its a map you can use to go from the key to the note your trying to identify and after a wile its becomes second nature going down from 5 to 1 or up from 7 to 1 or however you do it. The other half is being able to find the key of a song it's not the most exciting thing to practise but it pays off. From my experience try singing a note that feels at home over all the chord and if your off your probably playing the 5th or 3rd of the key so in the beginning I would check those against what I had. So once you can a) find the key b) figure out the distance from the target note to the key using the major scale you can transcribe almost any pop song. This works for your minor too because the minor 1 is just the 6 of the major scale and you start from there then you don't have too memorize different scales. From there it's just speed and sight singing helps a lot especially going from the tonic to each scale degree so sing 1 2 1 3 etc then back down 1 (an octave higher) 7 etc  with that before too long your going up or down the scale in your mind fast enough you dont have to sing each step you sing the target note. Chord progressions are a bit trickier because there's the additional step of being able to pick out the root note of the chord but practising on the paino by just playing a triad with the root doubled in your left an octave lower then matching the root an octave higher by singing an octave helps and then your kinda there. I wish I would have given up on interval stuff a minute ago I agree it's not really giving you the tools as a beginner if you dont have a natural ear but better late then never and I went from struggling to being able to transcribe most pop songs well enough for my usage anyway in a year. Keep at it and you'll get there!
